title: Acute Inflammatory Skin Conditions
subject: Integumentary System (INTG)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter explains the acute inflammatory rashes: atopic dermatitis, allergic and irritant contact dermatitis, erythema multiforme, urticaria and angioedema, Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis, pityriasis rosea, seborrheic dermatitis, and aphthous ulcers. Each one is an immune or barrier problem in a specific layer of the skin, and the layer involved predicts what the lesion looks like, how long it lasts, and what the biopsy shows. Board questions give a distribution, a time course, or a histologic description and expect you to name the mechanism. The most useful habit is to ask which cell is doing the damage and at what depth.
prerequisites: Epidermal layers, keratinocyte differentiation, and the cornified envelope (IN-1, IN-2)
Dermal vasculature, postcapillary venules, and the mechanism of edema formation
Hypersensitivity types I through IV, including mast cell and cytotoxic T cell effector pathways (IM-6)
Antigen presentation by dendritic cells, MHC class I and II, and T cell priming (IM-3)

connections.how: These rashes are the visible form of type I (urticaria), type IV (contact dermatitis), and cytotoxic T cell reactions (erythema multiforme, toxic epidermal necrolysis), so the skin becomes a readable model of each mechanism.
Atopic dermatitis shares its Th2 bias with allergic rhinitis and asthma, which is why sensitization through damaged skin can be followed by airway disease.

connections.to: Skin and systemic infections (IN-14, MI topics)
connections.how: Barrier failure invites Staphylococcus aureus and herpes simplex virus, and reactivation of HSV, HHV-6, HHV-7, and Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection triggers several of these eruptions.
Recurrent aphthous ulcers can be the first visible sign of Behcet disease, inflammatory bowel disease, or celiac disease.
Widespread epidermal loss in toxic epidermal necrolysis removes the water barrier, so the physiology of the burn patient explains the hypovolemia, heat loss, and sepsis risk.

sections.title: Atopic dermatitis: barrier failure and Th2 inflammation

blocks.text: Atopic dermatitis is a chronic, relapsing, intensely itchy dermatitis that begins in most patients before the age of five. Two defects drive it and each worsens the other: a leaky epidermal barrier and an immune system biased toward type 2 responses.

The barrier side begins in the stratum corneum. Filaggrin, encoded by FLG, aggregates keratin filaments into the dense bundles of the cornified cell and is then degraded into the small hydrophilic molecules known as natural moisturizing factor. Loss of function mutations in FLG, which are common in populations of European ancestry, therefore produce a corneal layer that is poorly cross linked and dry. Transepidermal water loss rises, surface pH rises, and allergens, haptens, and microbes penetrate to reach the Langerhans cells of the epidermis.

The immune side amplifies the defect. Injured keratinocytes release thymic stromal lymphopoietin, IL-25, and IL-33, which push dendritic cells to prime Th2 cells. IL-4 and IL-13 drive B cell class switching to IgE, which explains the raised serum IgE and eosinophilia, and they also suppress transcription of filaggrin, loricrin, and the antimicrobial peptides, so the barrier worsens because of the inflammation it caused. IL-31, also a Th2 product, acts on sensory neurons and is the main pruritogen, which matters because the itch responds poorly to antihistamines; histamine is not the principal mediator.

blocks.title: The itch and barrier cycle in atopic dermatitis
steps: Filaggrin loss raises water loss and lets allergens enter

Th2 cells make IL-4, IL-13, and IL-31

blocks.caption: Barrier failure and Th2 inflammation reinforce each other, so the disease is self sustaining until the loop is interrupted.

blocks.text: Distribution changes with age in a way that is heavily tested. Infants have weeping, crusted patches on the cheeks, scalp, and extensor limbs, and the diaper area is characteristically spared because it stays moist and is not scratched. From about age two the eruption moves into the flexures: the antecubital and popliteal fossae, neck, wrists, and ankles. Adults often have hand dermatitis, eyelid involvement, and thick plaques with exaggerated skin lines, the lichenification that follows years of rubbing.

rows: Cheeks, scalp, extensor limbs; diaper area spared

blocks.caption: The same disease looks different by age because the lesion reflects how long the skin has been scratched.

blocks.text: Atopic dermatitis is one third of the atopic triad with allergic rhinitis and asthma, and in many children it comes first, so sensitization through inflamed skin precedes airway disease. Two complications follow directly from the loss of antimicrobial peptides. Staphylococcus aureus colonizes lesional skin in most patients and its superantigens worsen inflammation, producing weeping, honey colored crusting, and flares. Eczema herpeticum is widespread herpes simplex infection of eczematous skin, recognized by monomorphic punched out erosions with scalloped borders, fever, and malaise, and it can disseminate.

blocks.predict: A child with severe eczema is exposed to a parent with a cold sore and develops hundreds of uniform, punched out erosions with fever. Why does atopic skin permit this when normal skin does not?
blocks.explain: Name the two defects that allow viral spread and say which cytokines created the second one.
blocks.check: Compare your answer with the paragraph on IL-4 and IL-13 suppression of antimicrobial peptides and the complications paragraph.

blocks.text: Contact dermatitis is inflammation caused by something that touched the skin. It comes in two forms that look similar at the bedside and are separated by whether the immune system learned the antigen first.

Allergic contact dermatitis is a delayed type (type IV) hypersensitivity reaction and requires two phases. In the sensitization phase, a small lipophilic chemical crosses the stratum corneum and acts as a hapten: it is too small to be recognized alone, so it binds covalently to self proteins. Langerhans cells, the dendritic cells of the epidermis, take up the modified protein, migrate to the regional lymph node, and present hapten-modified peptides to naive T cells, generating memory T cells over about one to two weeks. Nothing is visible during this phase. On re-exposure, skin homing memory CD4 and CD8 effectors return to the site and release interferon gamma and other cytokines that recruit more mononuclear cells. Because this requires cell recruitment rather than preformed mediators, the eruption appears about 48 to 72 hours after contact rather than within minutes.

blocks.caption: The first exposure teaches and the later exposure inflames, which is why a patient can wear an earring for years and then react to it.

blocks.text: The common allergens are worth knowing by name. Nickel is the most frequent, released from jewelry, buckles, and snaps when sweat corrodes the metal. Urushiol is the catechol oil of poison ivy, poison oak, and poison sumac, and it cross reacts among these plants and with mango skin and cashew shell. Other frequent sensitizers are fragrance mixes, preservatives, rubber accelerators in gloves, and topical neomycin. The patch test confirms the diagnosis: allergens are applied under occlusion and read at 48 hours and again at 72 to 96 hours, and a positive result is an itchy, indurated, sometimes vesicular reaction that persists or increases at the later reading.

Irritant contact dermatitis is more common overall and involves no immune memory. The agent injures keratinocytes directly, releasing IL-1 and other preformed cytokines, so it can occur on first exposure, it is dose and duration dependent, and anyone exposed to enough of the agent will react. Patients report burning and stinging more than itch, the skin looks dry, glazed, and fissured rather than vesicular, the margins are sharp at the limits of exposure, and the patch test is negative. Soaps, detergents, solvents, acids and alkalis, and repeated wetting are the usual causes.

blocks.title: Allergic versus irritant contact dermatitis
rows: Type IV hypersensitivity, hapten-specific T cells

Yes, sensitization phase of 1 to 2 weeks
Vesicles, edema, may spread beyond contact site

blocks.caption: Timing, itch versus burn, and the patch test separate the two forms; the lesion itself can be identical.

blocks.text: Two points prevent common errors. The eruption of allergic contact dermatitis can extend slightly beyond the contact site and occasionally becomes generalized because sensitized T cells circulate, while irritant dermatitis stays where the chemical was. Blister fluid in poison ivy dermatitis contains no urushiol, so the rash does not spread from scratching open vesicles; what spreads it is unwashed oil on hands, clothing, pets, or tools.

sections.title: Reading the exposure from the distribution, and the histology of eczema

blocks.text: Contact dermatitis is the one rash whose shape is a record of what touched the skin. Because the reaction occurs where antigen or irritant penetrated, the eruption reproduces the geometry of the exposure, and board questions use this in both directions: a described pattern should suggest an agent, and a named exposure should let you predict the pattern.

blocks.text: Two patterns are easy to confuse with contact dermatitis. A photoallergic or phototoxic reaction also involves exposed skin but spares shadowed sites, so the upper eyelids, the submental area, and the skin behind the ears are clear, and the eruption stops at the collar and sleeve lines. Airborne contact dermatitis involves those same shadowed areas. Dermatitis limited to the dorsa of the hands with sparing of the palms suggests an external agent, while symmetric involvement of palms and soles with deep itchy vesicles suggests dyshidrotic eczema instead.

The histologic hallmark of all eczematous dermatitis, allergic and irritant contact dermatitis included, is spongiosis. Inflammatory edema moves from the dermis into the epidermis and collects between keratinocytes, widening the intercellular spaces until the cells appear separated by clear fluid and connected only by stretched desmosomes. When enough fluid accumulates the desmosomes give way and the spaces coalesce into intraepidermal vesicles, which is why acute lesions weep. Lymphocytes migrate into the epidermis with the fluid, and a perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate with papillary dermal edema sits beneath.

The picture changes with duration, and the sequence explains the clinical appearance at each stage. Acute lesions are dominated by spongiosis and vesiculation and look red and weeping. Subacute lesions add parakeratosis, the retention of nuclei in the cornified layer that corresponds to visible scale and crust. Chronic lesions show acanthosis, hyperkeratosis, and hypergranulosis with little remaining spongiosis, the microscopic basis of lichenification. Spongiosis is not specific to contact dermatitis; it appears in atopic dermatitis, dyshidrotic eczema, and stasis dermatitis, so the diagnosis still depends on distribution and history.

sections.title: Erythema multiforme as a cytotoxic T cell reaction

blocks.text: Erythema multiforme is an acute, self limited, often recurrent eruption in which cytotoxic T cells kill keratinocytes at the dermoepidermal junction. It is an immune reaction to an infection in the great majority of cases, not a drug reaction, and this is the single most useful fact separating it from Stevens-Johnson syndrome.

Herpes simplex virus, usually HSV-1, causes most cases. Viral DNA fragments are carried by circulating mononuclear cells to the skin, where expressed viral antigen recruits HSV-specific CD4 cells that release interferon gamma, which amplifies local inflammation and brings in CD8 cells that kill antigen-bearing keratinocytes. The lesions therefore appear one to three weeks after the cold sore, at sites distant from it, and recur with each HSV reactivation; the virus is not replicating in the target lesions. Mycoplasma pneumoniae is the second major trigger, particularly in children, where it often produces more mucosal disease, and it should be suspected when the eruption follows a cough and fever.

blocks.title: Why target lesions follow a cold sore
steps: HSV reactivates at the lip and replicates
Mononuclear cells carry HSV DNA fragments to distant skin

HSV-specific CD4 cells release interferon gamma
CD8 cells kill antigen-bearing basal keratinocytes

blocks.caption: The rash is an immune response to viral antigen carried into the skin, so it is remote from the cold sore and recurs with it.

blocks.text: The lesion is the diagnosis. A typical target lesion is a round papule or plaque under about 3 cm across with three concentric zones: a dusky or blistered center where keratinocytes have died, a pale ring of edema, and an outer ring of erythema. Lesions appear abruptly over a few days, stay fixed for at least seven days, and favor acral and extensor skin, meaning the dorsal hands, palms, forearms, elbows, knees, and feet. They are symmetric and may burn or itch mildly rather than being painful. Mucosal disease is limited: erythema multiforme minor has none, and erythema multiforme major has erosions usually confined to the oral mucosa and lips with the patient otherwise well.

Histology shows interface dermatitis. Lymphocytes line up along the dermoepidermal junction, the basal layer vacuolizes, and individual necrotic keratinocytes appear within the epidermis, each sometimes ringed by lymphocytes, a picture called satellite cell necrosis. Edema in the papillary dermis beneath the dying basal cells lifts the epidermis and produces the pale middle ring of the target, and when the whole junction fails a subepidermal blister forms at the center. Necrosis is scattered and partial, which is why the epidermis stays attached, the Nikolsky sign is negative, and lesions heal without scarring over two to four weeks.

blocks.title: Reasoning from a target lesion
blocks.text: A healthy 24 year old reports a cold sore that healed ten days ago. He now has about forty symmetric, 1 to 2 cm round plaques on the dorsal hands, forearms, and knees, each with a dusky center, a pale ring, and a red outer ring, plus two small oral erosions. He feels well and takes no medication. Work backward: three concentric zones and acral distribution identify a target lesion; the dusky center means dead keratinocytes from cytotoxic T cell attack; distant timing after HSV identifies the trigger; limited mucosal disease and the absence of a drug and of systemic illness argue against Stevens-Johnson syndrome. The expected course is resolution in weeks, with recurrence at the next HSV reactivation.

sections.title: Urticaria, angioedema, and the two mediators of swelling

blocks.text: Urticaria is transient edema of the superficial dermis caused by mast cell degranulation. Histamine binds H1 receptors on the endothelium of postcapillary venules, which contract their endothelial cells and open interendothelial gaps, so plasma leaks into the dermis. The result is a wheal: a raised, pink, intensely itchy plaque with a pale center and a surrounding flare from axon reflex vasodilation. Because histamine is cleared within minutes and the fluid is reabsorbed, any individual wheal lasts less than 24 hours and leaves no mark, while new wheals appear elsewhere. A lesion that persists for days in one place, or that leaves bruising or scale, is not urticaria and suggests urticarial vasculitis.

Mast cells can be triggered three ways, and only the first is an allergy. IgE-mediated degranulation is type I hypersensitivity: antigen cross links IgE bound to FcepsilonRI, as with foods, beta lactams, and insect stings. Direct, non-IgE degranulation occurs when a substance activates the mast cell without antibody, as with opioids, vancomycin, and radiocontrast, so a reaction can occur on first exposure and skin testing is uninformative. Physical urticarias are reproducible responses to a stimulus: dermographism, cold, delayed pressure, solar, and cholinergic urticaria, in which a rise in core temperature produces small wheals with large flares. Aspirin and other nonselective cyclooxygenase inhibitors worsen urticaria by shifting arachidonic acid toward leukotrienes rather than by any immune mechanism.

Duration divides urticaria into acute, lasting under six weeks and usually following an infection, drug, or food, and chronic, lasting over six weeks. Chronic spontaneous urticaria has no external trigger in most patients, and many have IgG autoantibodies against IgE or FcepsilonRI itself that crosslink the receptor and keep mast cells releasing mediators; it is associated with autoimmune thyroid disease.

Angioedema is the same leak occurring deeper, in the lower dermis, subcutis, or submucosa, so the swelling is nonpitting, poorly demarcated, and tense rather than itchy, and it favors the eyelids, lips, tongue, genitals, hands, and feet. When it accompanies hives it is histamine driven, up to and including anaphylaxis. When it occurs without hives or itch it is usually bradykinin driven. C1 inhibitor restrains plasma kallikrein and factor XIIa as well as C1, so hereditary deficiency (low level in type 1, dysfunctional protein in type 2) lets kallikrein cleave high molecular weight kininogen into bradykinin, which raises permeability through endothelial B2 receptors. Attacks involve the face, larynx, and bowel wall, causing colic and vomiting, and antihistamines do not help. Unopposed C1 activity consumes C4, so a low C4 between attacks is the screening clue. Angiotensin converting enzyme is also kininase II, the main enzyme degrading bradykinin, so ACE inhibitors cause the same swelling by blocking its breakdown.

sections.title: Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis

blocks.text: Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis are two ends of one disease: widespread, full thickness necrosis of the epidermis caused by a drug-specific cytotoxic T cell response. They are separated only by how much skin detaches.

The mechanism is cytotoxic rather than inflammatory in the ordinary sense. A drug or its reactive metabolite is presented on MHC class I, so drug-specific CD8 T cells and natural killer cells accumulate in the epidermis. They kill keratinocytes by releasing granulysin, which is the most abundant cytotoxic protein in blister fluid, along with perforin and granzyme B, and by engaging Fas on keratinocytes with Fas ligand. Killing is diffuse and complete rather than scattered, so the entire epidermis dies and separates from the dermis at the level of the basement membrane. Susceptibility is partly genetic and HLA restricted, which explains why only a small fraction of exposed patients react; well established examples are HLA-B 15:02 with carbamazepine and HLA-B 58:01 with allopurinol.

The clinical course follows the mechanism. One to four weeks after a new drug is started, the patient develops fever, malaise, and sore eyes and mouth, then painful dusky macules and atypical flat targets that begin on the face and trunk, in contrast to the acral distribution of erythema multiforme. Pain out of proportion to the visible rash and mucosal erosions at two or more sites, typically oral, ocular, and genital, are the early warning signs. The epidermis then detaches in sheets, and the Nikolsky sign is positive because basal attachment, not just the intercellular junction, has failed. Classic triggers are sulfonamides, anticonvulsants such as carbamazepine, lamotrigine, and phenytoin, allopurinol, nevirapine, and oxicam nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. Mycoplasma pneumoniae can produce a similar picture with prominent mucositis, especially in children.

Losing the epidermis is physiologically equivalent to a large burn, which is where the mortality comes from. Water evaporates freely, so the patient becomes hypovolemic and loses heat, protein is lost in the exudate, and the denuded surface is invaded by Staphylococcus aureus and Pseudomonas, so sepsis and multiorgan failure follow. Mucosal necrosis extends to the conjunctiva, where healing can leave symblepharon and corneal scarring, and to the respiratory and genitourinary epithelium.

blocks.text: Two look-alikes are distinguished by the plane of separation. Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome results from exotoxins that cleave desmoglein 1, so the split is high in the epidermis beneath the stratum corneum, the mucosa is spared, and the patient is usually an infant or young child. Pemphigus vulgaris also splits within the epidermis, just above the basal layer, and shows acantholysis with intercellular IgG on immunofluorescence. Only Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis show necrosis of the whole epidermal thickness with separation at the dermoepidermal junction.

Pityriasis rosea is an acute, self limited papulosquamous eruption of adolescents and young adults, most common in spring and autumn. It is associated with systemic reactivation of human herpesvirus 6 and human herpesvirus 7, which accounts for the occasional prodrome of malaise, headache, mild fever, and sore throat in the week before the rash, and for the fact that it almost never recurs.

The eruption unfolds in two stages. First a herald patch appears, a single oval salmon pink to brown plaque about 2 to 10 cm across with a fine collarette of scale, usually on the trunk, neck, or proximal limb. Because it is solitary and annular it is commonly mistaken for tinea corporis, and a potassium hydroxide preparation that shows no hyphae settles the question. One to two weeks later the generalized eruption follows as crops of smaller oval papules and plaques with the same collarette scale, which is attached peripherally and free at its inner edge.

The arrangement is the examinable detail. The long axis of each oval lesion parallels the skin cleavage lines, the lines of Langer that reflect the predominant orientation of dermal collagen bundles. On the back the cleavage lines slope downward and laterally from the spine, so the lesions form the drooping branches described as a Christmas tree or fir tree pattern. The eruption concentrates on the trunk and proximal limbs and generally spares the face, palms, and soles. Itch is mild or absent, the patient feels well, and the lesions fade spontaneously over about six to eight weeks, sometimes leaving temporary postinflammatory hypopigmentation or hyperpigmentation in darker skin. Histology is nonspecific, showing focal spongiosis, mounds of parakeratosis, a perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate, and often extravasated red cells in the papillary dermis.

The distinction that matters most is from secondary syphilis, which can produce a similar scaly trunk eruption. Secondary syphilis characteristically involves the palms and soles, lacks a herald patch, and comes with generalized lymphadenopathy, mucous patches, or condylomata lata, so serologic testing is appropriate when those features are present or the eruption persists beyond a few months. Guttate psoriasis has thicker, silvery, non collarette scale and tends to follow streptococcal pharyngitis, and tinea corporis has an active scaling advancing border and a positive potassium hydroxide examination.

blocks.text: Seborrheic dermatitis is a chronic, relapsing dermatitis confined to skin rich in sebaceous glands. It is not an infection and it is not caused by poor hygiene; it is an inflammatory response to commensal Malassezia yeasts, chiefly Malassezia globosa and Malassezia restricta, living in sebum.

Malassezia species are lipid dependent and cannot synthesize their own fatty acids, so they secrete lipases that hydrolyze sebum triglycerides and take up the saturated fatty acids they need. The unsaturated fatty acids left behind, including oleic acid, are irritating to the stratum corneum: they disrupt the barrier, provoke keratinocyte cytokine release, and cause abnormal, hurried keratinization that appears as scale. Susceptibility depends more on the host response than on the yeast count, since Malassezia is present on everyone, which is why the disease tracks sebaceous activity and immune status rather than colonization alone.

steps: Sebaceous glands secrete triglyceride-rich sebum

blocks.caption: The lesion appears only where sebum is plentiful, which is why distribution maps sebaceous gland density.

blocks.text: Distribution therefore follows the sebaceous map: the scalp, eyebrows and glabella, nasolabial folds, external ear canals and retroauricular skin, beard area, central chest, and the intertriginous folds. The lesions are poorly defined pink to salmon patches with greasy yellow scale, in contrast to the sharply marginated plaques and dry silvery scale of psoriasis, and itch is mild. Dandruff is the same process limited to scalp scaling without obvious inflammation.

The incidence is bimodal, and both peaks follow androgen-driven sebum production. In infants, maternal and neonatal androgens keep sebaceous glands active for the first months, producing cradle cap, which is thick adherent yellow scale on the vertex with little itch, often with flexural and diaper area involvement, and which resolves as sebum output falls. After puberty sebum production rises again, and the adult form persists through life with remissions and flares. The relative quiet of childhood between these peaks is predicted by the low sebum output of that period.

Two associations are regularly tested because they are diagnostic signals. Severe, extensive, or treatment resistant seborrheic dermatitis is common in advanced HIV infection, where falling CD4 counts weaken T cell control of Malassezia, so a florid eruption in a young adult warrants HIV testing. Parkinson disease and other parkinsonism, including the drug induced form, is associated with facial seborrhea and an oily facies, attributed to autonomic dysfunction and increased sebum output. Seborrheic dermatitis is also more frequent and more severe after stroke and in other conditions that limit facial movement.

sections.title: Recurrent aphthous ulcers and their systemic associations

blocks.text: Aphthous ulcers, called canker sores, are painful shallow ulcers of the oral mucosa produced by a T cell mediated attack on the epithelium rather than by any infectious agent. They are the most common ulcerative condition of the mouth.

The lesion begins as a tender red macule that breaks down within a day into a round or oval ulcer with a shallow crater, a yellow gray fibrinous base, and a sharply defined erythematous halo. Pain is out of proportion to size because the exposed submucosa carries dense sensory innervation. Histology shows a nonspecific ulcer with fibrinopurulent exudate and a mononuclear infiltrate, with CD8 cells predominating at the ulcer base, and the absence of viral cytopathic change or acantholysis distinguishes it from herpetic and autoimmune blistering lesions.

Location is the most reliable discriminator on an examination. Aphthous ulcers occur only on nonkeratinized, movable mucosa: the buccal and labial mucosa, the floor of the mouth, the ventral and lateral tongue, and the soft palate. They spare the keratinized surfaces, meaning the hard palate, the attached gingiva, and the dorsal tongue. Intraoral recurrent herpes simplex does the reverse, favoring keratinized hard palate and gingiva, and herpes labialis sits on the vermilion border. Primary herpetic gingivostomatitis presents with fever, diffuse gingival swelling, and clustered vesicles that coalesce, which aphthae never do.

blocks.text: Isolated minor aphthae in an otherwise well patient are usually idiopathic, with precipitants including local trauma, stress, menstrual hormonal change, sodium lauryl sulfate in toothpaste, and stopping smoking. Frequent, severe, or major ulcers, or ulcers with systemic symptoms, point to an underlying cause. Behcet disease is the classic association: recurrent oral and genital ulceration, uveitis, skin lesions such as pseudofolliculitis and erythema nodosum, and a positive pathergy test, driven by a vasculitis of vessels of all sizes and linked to HLA-B51. Inflammatory bowel disease, especially Crohn disease, produces aphthous ulcers both as an extraintestinal manifestation and through malabsorption, and celiac disease does the same, sometimes before any gastrointestinal symptom. Common to the malabsorptive causes is deficiency of iron, folate, vitamin B12, or zinc, which impairs epithelial turnover. Other causes include cyclic neutropenia, with ulcers recurring at the neutrophil nadir about every three weeks, HIV infection, and the childhood syndrome of periodic fever with aphthous stomatitis, pharyngitis, and adenitis.

integration.text: These eight conditions are best held together by depth and effector cell. In the superficial dermis, mast cell histamine opens venular gaps and produces a wheal that resolves in hours, while the same leak in deep dermis and subcutis is angioedema; replace the mediator with bradykinin and the itch and the hives disappear, which is immunology read directly off the skin. Within the epidermis, fluid between keratinocytes is spongiosis, the common histology of atopic and contact dermatitis, and it explains weeping vesicles. At the dermoepidermal junction, cytotoxic T cells produce interface dermatitis: scattered keratinocyte death gives the fixed target lesion of erythema multiforme, and confluent full thickness necrosis gives the detaching sheets of toxic epidermal necrolysis. Pathology supplies the plane of separation that names a blistering disease, immunology supplies the cell, and anatomy supplies the layer.

Several threads run outward into other disciplines. Barrier biochemistry links filaggrin and the cornified envelope to transepidermal water loss, and the loss of antimicrobial peptides under IL-4 and IL-13 connects a genetic barrier defect to Staphylococcus aureus colonization and eczema herpeticum, which is microbiology following from physiology. Microbial triggers run through the whole chapter: HSV in erythema multiforme, HHV-6 and HHV-7 in pityriasis rosea, Malassezia in seborrheic dermatitis, and Mycoplasma pneumoniae in both erythema multiforme and Stevens-Johnson syndrome, and in each case the organism is not destroying tissue but provoking an immune response, so cultures of the rash are unhelpful. Where lesions in the mouth are concerned, gastroenterology and rheumatology matter as much as dermatology. The limits are worth stating plainly: histology in several of these conditions, including pityriasis rosea and aphthous ulceration, is nonspecific, so the diagnosis rests on distribution and time course, and immunologic classification is imperfect because chronic spontaneous urticaria and erythema multiforme both involve mechanisms that do not fit neatly into one hypersensitivity type.

summary: Atopic dermatitis is filaggrin-related barrier failure plus Th2 inflammation; IL-4 and IL-13 lower filaggrin and antimicrobial peptides, and IL-31 drives itch, so antihistamines help little.

Atopic dermatitis affects the face and extensors in infants and the flexures later, with lichenification from chronic scratching, and it predisposes to Staphylococcus aureus infection and eczema herpeticum.

Allergic contact dermatitis is type IV hypersensitivity requiring hapten sensitization through Langerhans cells and appearing 48 to 72 hours after re-exposure with a positive patch test; irritant dermatitis is direct keratinocyte injury with no sensitization and a negative patch test.
Contact dermatitis reproduces the shape of the exposure, and spongiosis, which is intercellular epidermal edema, is the histologic hallmark of all eczematous dermatitis.

Erythema multiforme is cytotoxic T cell killing of keratinocytes, usually after HSV and sometimes after Mycoplasma pneumoniae, giving fixed acral three-zone target lesions, limited mucosal disease, and interface dermatitis with scattered necrotic keratinocytes.
Each urticarial wheal lasts under 24 hours because histamine opens venular gaps transiently; chronic urticaria lasts over 6 weeks and often involves IgG autoantibodies to IgE or its receptor.
Angioedema without hives or itch is bradykinin mediated: C1 inhibitor deficiency with a low C4, or ACE inhibition blocking bradykinin breakdown, and antihistamines do not work.

Stevens-Johnson syndrome (under 10 percent detached) and toxic epidermal necrolysis (over 30 percent) are drug-triggered CD8 and granulysin-mediated full thickness epidermal necrosis with severe mucosal disease and a positive Nikolsky sign; losing the epidermis causes burn-like fluid loss and sepsis.

Pityriasis rosea follows HHV-6 and HHV-7 reactivation: a herald patch, then oval collarette-scaled patches along cleavage lines in a Christmas tree pattern, resolving in 6 to 8 weeks; palmoplantar involvement suggests secondary syphilis instead.

Seborrheic dermatitis is inflammation from Malassezia lipase products in sebaceous skin, with greasy yellow scale and infant cradle cap, and severe disease points to HIV infection or Parkinson disease; aphthous ulcers occur only on nonkeratinized mucosa and recur in Behcet disease, inflammatory bowel disease, and celiac disease.

verify: The prevalence of filaggrin loss of function mutations in atopic dermatitis varies widely by population and source (roughly 20 to 50 percent of patients of European ancestry); confirm whether NABNE expects any figure.

Mortality estimates for Stevens-Johnson syndrome (about 10 percent) and toxic epidermal necrolysis (about 30 percent, with some series higher) differ between references; the figures here are consensus approximations.
The proportion of chronic spontaneous urticaria with functional autoantibodies to IgE or FcepsilonRI is quoted from about 30 to 50 percent; confirm the value expected.
The reported proportion of erythema multiforme attributable to HSV ranges from about 50 to over 90 percent depending on whether recurrent cases are included.
HLA associations for severe cutaneous drug reactions (HLA-B 15:02 with carbamazepine, HLA-B 58:01 with allopurinol) are population specific; confirm whether Part I tests them.

The mechanism linking Parkinson disease to facial seborrhea is still debated (increased sebum output, autonomic dysfunction, and reduced facial movement are all proposed); it is stated here as association with proposed mechanisms.
Whether NABNE Part I expects the eponyms Langer cleavage lines, Nikolsky sign, Behcet disease, and the PFAPA syndrome, or only descriptive terms, should be checked.

Requested new diagram names for a future revision: skin-split-levels (subcorneal, intraepidermal, subepidermal separation planes side by side with the diseases at each level), spongiosis-vs-interface (eczematous versus interface histology), and wheal-versus-angioedema (depth of dermal edema in each).

Classification of erythema multiforme and Stevens-Johnson syndrome as separate diseases follows current consensus, but some older references treat erythema multiforme major and Stevens-Johnson syndrome as a single entity; confirm the framing NABNE uses.
